text: A group has the \emph{unique-product property} if, for every pair of finite nonempty subsets \(P,Q\), some element of \(PQ\) has exactly one expression \(pq\) with \(p\in P\), \(q\in Q\). Applying this property to the supports of two nonzero group-algebra elements gives a nonzero product coefficient. Rips and Segev constructed torsion-free groups without unique product~\cite{RipsSegev1987}; Steenbock supplied a graphical small-cancellation treatment of their construction~\cite{Steenbock2015}. Mian and Siddique report a machine-checked non-unique-product witness for Gardam's \(\widetilde A_2\) lattice, taking torsion-freeness from Gardam rather than formalizing it~\cite[Sections~1 and~7]{MianSiddique2026}. Failure of unique product alone does not produce a zero divisor: over \(\mathbb F_2\), the relevant representation counts must be even, not merely greater than one.
